extracted.intended_audience: students in C409 News Media Ethics / journalism students
extracted.subtask_description: Reflective student-blog guidance and evaluative criteria about ethical journalism, focusing on honesty, verification, accountability, and editorial responsibility illustrated by the Stephen Glass / Shattered Glass case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty / Seek truth and report it
rubrics_metrics.description: “Honesty is something that isn’t optional in the journalistic world, it’s a duty...” and the SPJ principle to “seek truth and report it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students repeatedly frame honesty as the core duty of journalists: reporting factually, not mixing fiction with fact. Examples: Stephen Glass’s fabrication violated this duty. Scoring/assessment note: central, disqualifying breach when absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take responsibility for accuracy / Verify information before releasing it
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct guidance: “Take responsibility for the accuracy of their work. Verify information before releasing it” (SPJ quoted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes individual reporter obligations to check facts and confirm sources prior to publication. Anti-pattern: bypassing fact-checks or forging notes to simulate verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be accountable and transparent; admit and correct errors
rubrics_metrics.description: “Be accountable and transparent” and American Press Institute: “We invite the public to report errors and request corrections, and we publicly admit our errors.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers and reporters should publicly acknowledge mistakes and issue corrections. Example: Glass failed to admit errors when exposed. Practically, transparency about methods and corrections rebuilds trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fabrication and made-up sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit prohibition against fabricated stories and sources — page documents Glass “fabricated 27 of his 41 stories” and created “fake websites, documents, notes, fake voicemails, fake faxes.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: all reported facts and sources must be verifiable. Anti-patterns include inventing people/places, forging notes, creating false contact info or websites to support claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect credibility and public trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple posts state: credibility/integrity is paramount (e.g., “credibility is everything,” “Integrity and credibility is the most precious treasure of all the journalists”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation: weigh how actions affect audience trust and organizational reputation. Fabrication or persistent inaccuracy is judged as destroying credibility; restoring trust is difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor responsibility and editorial oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim: “Any fact-checking system is built on trust... the real vetting system is not fact-checking but the editor. It’s the editor’s responsibility to spot red flags.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assigns a duty to editors to detect anomalies and implement safeguards beyond relying solely on reporter honesty. Examples: editors should look for patterns that suggest fabrication and intervene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about standards, methods, and motivations
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted: “Trust in a professional approach requires transparency about standards, methods and motivations – and a culture which prizes accuracy and a positive relationship with the public.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsrooms should disclose reporting methods and decision rationales where relevant. This supports accountability and allows audiences to judge journalistic rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zero-tolerance and appropriate consequences for fabrication
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments for strict consequences: e.g., “break the trust once, and you never will write non-fiction again” and suggestions that those who invent facts “should be fired.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides organizational disciplinary policy: deliberate fabrication should prompt severe sanctions (dismissal, public censure) to protect institutional credibility. Some nuance in student reflections about second chances, but default is strict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness and loyalty to colleagues / workplace responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethical values include loyalty and fairness; Glass’s deception “betrayed his audience and his co-workers,” violating obligations to colleagues as well as readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment includes interpersonal harms in newsroom: deceit that advantages one reporter over coworkers (e.g., career advancement via false stories) is unethical and damages workplace morale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not abuse or game the fact-checking system
rubrics_metrics.description: Students note Glass “used his knowledge of how the fact checking system works and abused it,” bypassing safeguards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: reporters must not exploit procedural gaps (e.g., submitting forged verification artifacts). Organizations should close such loopholes and verify independently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid prioritizing personal gain over ethical reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Explains motives: liars “lie to protect themselves, look good, gain financially or socially and avoid punishment” (Spurlock/Saltz).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation considers whether reporter prioritized fame, social acceptance, or career advancement over accuracy. Ethical practice requires subordinating personal ambition to truth and public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use modern verification tools and available resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that today Glass “would not have been able to forge the many articles he wrote as every word could be searched in a second.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically: employ digital verification (searches, metadata checks, contact verifications) and training to prevent fabrication and detect anomalies that older systems missed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote public interest and moral culture beyond mere legality
rubrics_metrics.description: Statement: journalists must “promote public interests and knowledge and to have a moral culture that goes beyond the legal requirements already in place.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for judging reporting: obligations to public service and ethical norms can exceed minimum legal compliance; evaluate reporting by public-interest contribution and moral responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of rehabilitation / rehiring after ethical breaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate about allowing people back into journalism after lying; e.g., “does it make sense to allow people back into journalism who have a track record of lying?” and personal stance: reluctance to rehire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides hiring and reinstatement decisions: weigh risk to colleagues and audience, evidence of genuine remediation, and potential ongoing harm. Some student positions recommend permanent exclusion in high-trust roles.
